senses.definition: Synonym of supremum.

core.definition: In mathematics, the smallest value that is greater than or equal to every element of a set. It is also called the supremum.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BOUND, the last word, while LEAST and UPPER get secondary stress. The r in UPPER is American and reduced, so the word ends in a soft schwa-r sound rather than a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in real analysis, calculus and proof-based courses, and in discussions of the completeness of the real numbers. Many textbooks prefer the shorter word supremum, but in a US classroom you will hear both. Students usually learn the phrase before the symbol sup, and the two terms are interchangeable.

distinctions.note: A maximum must itself belong to the set, while a least upper bound need not; the open interval (0,1) has no maximum but its least upper bound is 1.
The two terms name the same object; supremum is the shorter, more common term in many texts, while least upper bound is more descriptive for beginners.
Any number at or above every element of the set is an upper bound; the least upper bound is the smallest such number.

collocations: least upper bound of the set
bounded above by its least upper bound
prove the least upper bound exists

examples.everyday: My daughter asked what a least upper bound is, and I honestly needed a whiteboard to explain it.
examples.professional: Before we submit the proof to the review team, we need to show that the least upper bound exists for this bounded set.
examples.analytical: The completeness axiom guarantees that every nonempty set of real numbers bounded above has a least upper bound.

nuance.analogy: Like the lowest ceiling that still clears everyone standing in a room: any higher ceiling works too, but this one is the smallest that still does.
nuance.etymology: Built from English least, upper and bound (boundary, from Old French bonde); the phrase was coined in mathematical English as a descriptive term.
common_mistakes: Confusing least upper bound with maximum, assuming the bound must be an element of the set.
Saying the least upper bound is the lowest number in the set; it is the smallest number that is above every element.

senses.definition: A Lebanese or Middle Eastern person.

core.definition: An informal and sometimes offensive short form for a Lebanese person or a person of Lebanese descent.

pronunciation.tip: It is a single syllable with a short e as in 'bed' and a clear final b. Do not stretch it into a longer word like 'Lee-ban'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it can be derogatory, and many Lebanese Americans find it offensive.
nuance.usage_note: Some young people use Leb casually among friends, but it is risky in mixed company and can sound disrespectful or stereotyping. In writing, workplaces, and polite conversation, say Lebanese or Lebanese American. Middle Eastern is a broader geographic term and does not mean the same as Lebanese.

distinctions.note: Lebanese is the respectful and standard term for people from Lebanon or of Lebanese descent.
Middle Eastern is a broad regional label that covers many countries and peoples, not just Lebanese people.
Arab usually refers to language and culture shared across many countries, while Lebanese names a specific nationality.

examples.everyday: Some guys on my team call that family down the street the Lebs, but I always say Lebanese.
examples.professional: In the community report, please use Lebanese rather than informal slang, which can sound offensive.
examples.analytical: The clipped form Leb carries an ethnic shorthand that can flatten a diverse community into a single stereotype.

nuance.analogy: Using Leb is like calling someone by a nickname they never chose: it can sound friendly to one person and insulting to another.
nuance.etymology: A clipped informal form of Lebanese.
common_mistakes: Using Leb as a neutral synonym for Lebanese in formal or professional writing.
Assuming Leb means any Middle Eastern person; it refers specifically to Lebanese people.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a legend or to legends.
senses.example: The professor's lecture covered the legendary origins of the Norse gods and their stories.

senses.definition: Appearing (solely) in legends.
senses.example: Few scholars believe the legendary dragon ever existed outside the medieval tales.

senses.definition: Having the splendor of a legend; fabled.
senses.example: The wedding reception at the old estate felt legendary, with gold candles and endless champagne.

senses.definition: Having unimaginable greatness; excellent to such an extent to evoke stories.
senses.example: Her legendary patience with difficult students made her the favorite teacher in the whole district.

senses.definition: A legendary Pokémon.
senses.example: My nephew spent the entire afternoon trying to catch the legendary Pokémon hidden in the cave.

core.definition: Very famous, celebrated, or widely known, often for achievements or qualities that people talk about for years.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LEJ, with a weaker secondary stress on DAIR. The -ary ending is a reduced syllable, pronounced like 'air-ee' in American speech, not 'ary' with a long a.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a person, a thing, or an event, and it can sound exaggerated if used for ordinary things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use legendary for food, sports figures, musicians, bosses, and even local places, often with a light, friendly tone. It is often used with a little humor, as in legendary grumpiness. In formal writing, it can refer to myths or traditional tales, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Famous is the neutral word for being well known. Legendary suggests greater renown built over time, often with admiration.
Mythical means existing only in myth or imagination. Legendary can mean famous or that the stories about a person are part of the lore.

examples.everyday: Her cheesecake is legendary at every church potluck, and people ask for the recipe every year.
examples.professional: The engineer's legendary debugging skills are why the team called her when production went down.
examples.analytical: Scholars note that the legendary exploits of the hero were shaped by generations of retelling rather than by documented events.

nuance.analogy: Like a famous landmark that everyone in town has a story about, long after the first builders are gone.
nuance.etymology: Formed from legend, from Medieval Latin legenda (things to be read).
common_mistakes: Using legendary as a noun in the sense of a famous person; in English, legendary is an adjective, and the noun is legend.
Stressing the last syllable, as in LEJ-un-dair-EE.

senses.definition: The quality of being liberal.
Any political movement founded on the autonomy and personal freedom of the individual, progress and reform, and government by law with the consent of the governed.
senses.example: Classical liberalism shaped the constitutional debates about individual rights and government consent.

senses.definition: An economic ideology in favor of laissez faire and the free market (related to economic liberalism).
senses.example: Her economics seminar compared economic liberalism with state-directed planning and protectionist tariffs.

senses.definition: A school of international relations that emphasizes cooperation (such as trade) between polities, as an alternative to power politics, and the geopolitically transformative role of democratization, as opposed to inherent structural material factors.
senses.example: Her international relations professor defended liberalism as a path to cooperation between states.

core.definition: A political philosophy that values individual liberty, equal rights under law, and government by the consent of the governed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LIB, and keep the -ism ending weak, like uhm. Learners often stress the -ISM or pronounce the second syllable as 'bee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for supporters; negative when critics use it as a label for big government or social change, so it depends on the audience.
nuance.usage_note: In American politics, liberalism often means the progressive left on issues like civil rights and healthcare, while economists may use it for free-market ideas, so ask which sense is intended. Use it as a general term in academic talk, and be careful in casual conversation, where it can sound like a party label. Americans say classical liberalism for the older idea of limited government.

distinctions.note: Liberal is the adjective or a person who holds the views; liberalism is the belief system behind them.
Conservatism emphasizes tradition and gradual change; liberalism emphasizes individual rights and reform.
Libertarianism wants much less government, while liberalism accepts a larger role for government in protecting rights.

examples.everyday: We argued about liberalism over dinner, but honestly we mostly disagreed about taxes.
examples.professional: Her policy memo applies liberalism's commitment to individual rights to the proposed privacy regulation.
examples.analytical: Liberalism rests on the claim that legitimate government depends on the consent of the governed, not on tradition or divine right.

nuance.analogy: Liberalism is like a referee's rulebook: it sets fair terms so everyone can compete freely, even when they disagree about who should win.
nuance.etymology: From liberal plus -ism, from Latin liberalis 'of a free person'.
common_mistakes: Using liberalism and liberal interchangeably; liberalism names the ideology, while liberal names the adjective or a supporter.
Assuming the word means the same thing as the modern US party label; its meaning has shifted over the centuries.

senses.definition: A central defender to whom no forward is assigned for marking, forming the last line of defense and often initiating the offensive play.
senses.example: The libero stayed near the back line, ready to cover any breakthrough by the forwards.

senses.definition: A designated back-row player intended to be used as a ball-control specialist.
senses.example: Our libero received almost every serve, and her passes set up the middle hitter.

core.definition: In volleyball, a back-row defensive specialist in a contrasting jersey who can substitute freely and cannot attack above the net.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LIB. Americans do not use the Italian pronunciation, lee-beh-roh, which is a common error.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It is praise when a team has a strong libero and simply a role name otherwise.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, libero almost always means a volleyball player, and coaches and fans use it casually at high school, college and club levels. In soccer, Americans usually say sweeper for the same kind of defensive role. A natural comment is 'Our libero is the best passer on the team.'

distinctions.note: Sweeper is the common American soccer term for a defender who covers behind the back line. Libero is the same concept, but the word is used mainly for volleyball.
A middle blocker plays at the net and focuses on blocking and quick attacks. A libero stays in the back row and focuses on defense and passing.

examples.everyday: My daughter plays libero on her club team, and she loves diving for balls.
examples.professional: Our coaching staff tracks each libero's serve-receive accuracy because it drives our offense.
examples.analytical: The libero rule reshaped volleyball by separating defensive skill from attacking height, which changed how coaches recruited players.

nuance.analogy: A libero is like a goalkeeper on the back-row side of a volleyball court: they keep the ball alive so the team can attack.
nuance.etymology: From Italian libero, 'free,' because the role is not tied to a fixed position.
common_mistakes: Using Italian pronunciation, lee-beh-roh, instead of LIB-uh-roh.
Thinking that any back-row player is a libero. The libero is a specific rostered role with a different jersey.

senses.definition: A tower or other structure exhibiting a light or lights to warn or guide sailors.
senses.example: In the history of lighthouses, English civil engineer John Smeaton made a significant contribution to the design of them.

core.definition: A tall tower on a coast, with a powerful light that warns or guides ships away from rocks and into harbors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LYT, and the final syllable rhymes with 'mouse', not 'hoes'. The h is clearly pronounced between the two parts, and the word is one word, not two.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests safety, guidance and hope, and it is often used figuratively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lighthouse in everyday talk about coastal trips, tourism and history, such as visiting an old lighthouse on the coast of Maine. Figuratively, it can mean a source of guidance or hope, as in 'She was a lighthouse for the team during the crisis.' Writers spell it as one word, and two-word spellings are not standard. A natural remark on a trip is 'Let's climb to the top of the lighthouse.'

distinctions.note: A beacon is any light or signal used to guide, and it is often used figuratively; a lighthouse is a specific tower on a coast.
A lightship is a ship with a light that serves as a floating lighthouse, usually where a tower cannot be built.

examples.everyday: Let's drive out to the point and see the old lighthouse before the sun goes down.
examples.professional: The coast guard's navigation team updated the lighthouse signals so that they match the new nautical charts.
examples.analytical: In Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse, the lighthouse becomes a symbol of a distant, unreachable truth that the characters keep trying to approach.

nuance.analogy: Like a fixed star on a dark sea: it does not move, and it tells travelers where safe ground lies.
nuance.etymology: From light (noun) plus house, meaning a building, with the sense of a structure that houses a light.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, 'light-HOUSE'; in American speech the stress falls on LYT.
Saying 'light house' as two words in formal writing, where the one-word form is standard.

senses.definition: Descent in a line from a common progenitor; progeny; descending line of offspring or ascending line of parentage.
senses.example: She traced her family's lineage back to a farmer who arrived in Virginia in 1650.

senses.definition: A number of lines of text in a column.
senses.example: The classified section printed each ad with a fixed lineage of eight lines.

senses.definition: A fee or rate paid per line of text.
senses.example: The paper raised its lineage rate to two dollars per line this year.

core.definition: The line of descent from a common ancestor, or the family history that connects a person to their ancestors.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, LIN. The final -age is an unstressed ij sound, not "ahj," and the middle i is quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, with a sense of heritage
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "lineage" to discuss family history, ancestry, or heritage, especially in formal or respectful contexts. It is common in genealogy, religion, and history. In casual talk people often say "family line" or "family tree." In data science, the term also refers to tracking where data came from.

distinctions.note: "Ancestry" stresses the origins of a person's forebears, while "lineage" stresses the continuous line of descent.
"Heritage" can include culture and traditions as well as ancestors, while "lineage" focuses on family descent.

examples.everyday: My grandmother loved telling us about our family lineage, going back to the farm in Ohio.
examples.professional: The data team needs to document the lineage of each dataset so auditors can trace every transformation.
examples.analytical: The theologian traces the lineage of the doctrine through the early church fathers to show how it developed.

nuance.analogy: Lineage is like a river's path: every branch you see today flows from one source upstream.
nuance.etymology: From Old French lignage, from ligne, line, from Latin linea.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, which makes the word sound French.
Confusing "lineage" with "linage," the publishing term for payment per line, which is a different sense.

lineage.etymology: From Middle English *linage*, from Old French *linage*, from *ligne*, from Latin *linea* (“line”); equivalent to *line* + *-age*.

senses.definition: Someone who fits a lining to something.
senses.example: a liner of shoes

senses.definition: A removable cover or lining.
senses.example: I threw out the trash can liner.

senses.definition: The pamphlet supplied in the box with an audiovisual tape or disc, etc.
senses.example: liner notes

senses.definition: A lining within the cylinder of a steam engine, in which the piston works and between which and the outer shell of the cylinder a space is left to form a steam jacket.
senses.example: The engineer replaced the cracked liner inside the steam engine's cylinder before restarting the boiler.

senses.definition: A similar lining for cylinders of internal-combustion engines.
senses.example: The mechanic pressed a new cylinder liner into the engine block during the rebuild.

senses.definition: A slab on which small pieces of marble, tile, etc. are fastened for grinding.
senses.example: The craftsman mounted the marble fragments on a liner before grinding the tabletop smooth.

senses.definition: A formal no-show sock.
senses.example: He wore black dress liners under his loafers so his ankles stayed hidden.

senses.definition: A pantyliner.
senses.example: She tucked a thin liner into her underwear before the long hike.

senses.definition: A large passenger-carrying ship, especially one on a regular route; an ocean liner.
senses.example: Our grandparents crossed the Atlantic on a liner in 1958, sailing from Southampton to New York.

senses.definition: A basic salesperson.
senses.example: The store hired a liner to handle the basic models while senior staff worked the premium accounts.

senses.definition: Something with a specified number of lines.
senses.example: The bawdy limerick was a five-liner that the students recited at every party.

senses.definition: A person born in a certain year (XX liner); a person who belongs to a certain line.
senses.example: 94 liner

senses.definition: Ellipsis of penny-a-liner.
A ship of the line.
senses.example: The admiral's seventy-four-gun liner anchored in the harbor while the fleet prepared for battle.

senses.definition: A line drive.
senses.example: The liner glanced off the pitcher's foot.

senses.definition: To fit a cylinder liner.
senses.example: The shop will liner the worn cylinders so the engine can be rebuilt before spring.

core.definition: A removable cover or lining that protects or fits inside something, such as a trash can liner or a shelf liner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, LYE-ner. The final syllable is a weak, r-colored vowel, so do not pronounce it as LYE-nah or LYE-nee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word is practical and describes objects, not feelings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say trash can liner for the plastic bag inside a bin, and shelf liner or drawer liner for paper or plastic that covers the surface. The British term bin bag is not used in American speech. Liner also has other meanings, such as eyeliner in cosmetics and ocean liner for a large passenger ship.

distinctions.note: A lining is an inner layer sewn or attached inside something, such as a coat, while a liner is usually a separate piece that can be removed.
An ocean liner is a large passenger ship, while a liner in the sense of a cover is a small object you put inside something.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a new liner for the kitchen trash can? This one is full.
examples.professional: Order a heavier liner for the storage bins before the warehouse inspection next week.
examples.analytical: The critic treats the album's liner notes as a second text that frames how listeners hear the songs.

nuance.analogy: A trash can liner is like a protective inner bag in a box: it guards the container and comes out when it is full.
nuance.etymology: From the verb line plus the agent suffix -er, meaning something that lines.
common_mistakes: Using liner for a clothing lining; a coat has a lining, not a liner, unless it is a removable insert.
Pronouncing the final syllable with a clear ah sound instead of a weak r-colored vowel.

senses.definition: A type of storage compartment with a lock, usually used to store personal possessions for public use, such as in schools, railway stations, place of work, gyms, sports centers.
senses.example: The student placed her books in her locker when she arrived at school.

senses.definition: A lockable cubicle.
senses.example: She was afraid to come out of the locker.

senses.definition: A storage compartment on a ship, not necessarily one that can be locked.
senses.example: The crew stored their rain gear in a locker below the main deck.

senses.definition: A locking differential.
senses.example: The rally car has a locker in the rear axle for better traction on gravel.

senses.definition: A closet.
senses.example: After the party, she hung her coat in the locker by the front door.

senses.definition: An online storage service for files.
senses.example: I back up my thesis photos to a cloud locker every Sunday night.

senses.definition: (rare) One who locks something.
senses.example: The locker of the trapped chest must be careful, so as not to spring the trap.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (historical) A customs officer who guards a warehouse.
senses.example: In the eighteenth century, the locker watched over goods stored in the port warehouse.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A small storage compartment with a lock, used to keep personal belongings in a school, gym, or workplace.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a light, r-colored vowel. Learners often give the first vowel a long 'oh' sound, but it is the short 'ah' of 'lot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a practical everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'locker' for school hallways, gyms, and workplaces where people store coats or bags. Some schools and offices use open cubbies with no door, which Americans call cubbies or cubbyholes, not lockers. A common phrase is 'Meet me at my locker.'

distinctions.note: A cubby is an open compartment without a door or lock, often used in preschools, while a locker has a door and a lock.
A cabinet is a general storage piece that may hold anything, while a locker is usually a personal compartment for one user.

examples.everyday: I left my gym bag in my locker, so I'll grab it after my run.
examples.professional: Please label your locker with your name and return the key to the front desk at the end of your shift.
examples.analytical: The locker is a small private space within a public institution, and it shows how schools balance security with personal dignity.

nuance.analogy: Like a personal safe-deposit box that you can reach from the hallway.
nuance.etymology: From lock plus the agent suffix -er, meaning a thing that locks.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'LOH-ker' with a long o.
Using 'locker' for an open shelf or cubby with no lock.

senses.definition: One who disputes the meanings of words.

core.definition: A person who argues about the meanings of words, often to avoid the real question.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, GAH, and reduce the 'mach' part to 'muh-k' with a hard k sound. The word ends with a clear '-ist'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone who wins arguments by controlling terms rather than engaging ideas.
nuance.usage_note: This word is uncommon and mostly appears in philosophy, theology, law and literary writing. Americans would more likely describe such a person as someone who 'hairsplits' or 'nitpicks over words'. Use it carefully, since it sounds sharp and can be an insult.

distinctions.note: A pedant insists on correct rules and details, while a logomachist fights over what the words themselves mean.
Logomachic is an adjective describing a dispute, while logomachist is the noun for the person who starts it.

examples.everyday: My grandfather was a real logomachist who would argue for an hour about whether 'ain't' counts as a word.
examples.professional: Don't be a logomachist in code reviews; argue about behavior, not about whether a variable should be called 'user' or 'account'.
examples.analytical: A logomachist can win an argument by contesting the meaning of key terms rather than engaging the claim itself.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who argues over the label on a jar and never tastes what is inside.
nuance.etymology: From Greek logomachia, a fight about words, from logos (word) and machē (battle).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllables as 'mack' with a long a; the vowel is reduced.
Using it as a general word for a debater; it refers specifically to someone who disputes word meanings.

senses.definition: An adapter-based technique for efficiently fine-tuning models. An adapter.
senses.example: We used LoRA to fine-tune the language model on our customer support transcripts without retraining all its weights.

senses.definition: An adapter.
senses.example: The LoRA we trained for the medical model adds only a few megabytes to the base checkpoint.

core.definition: A method that fine-tunes a large AI model by training small low-rank matrices added to frozen weights, reducing memory and compute needs.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one word with stress on the first syllable, with a clear rhotic r. Do not spell it out as L-O-R-A, because Americans say it as a word, not as letters.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and AI, Americans say LOR-uh in team meetings, papers, and code discussions. Keep the capitalization LoRA, since the name comes from Low-Rank Adaptation. Non-specialists rarely use it, so explain it briefly if needed.

distinctions.note: Full fine-tuning updates all model weights and needs much more memory; LoRA freezes the original weights and trains only small added matrices.
Prompt tuning learns soft prompt vectors at the input; LoRA changes internal weight updates through low-rank matrices.

collocations: merge a LoRA into the base model

examples.everyday: My friend trained a LoRA so his photos look like watercolors, and it only took an afternoon.
examples.professional: We can use a LoRA to adapt the base model to our support tickets without retraining all the weights.
examples.analytical: A LoRA constrains the update to a low-rank subspace, which limits how far the model can drift from its pretrained behavior.

nuance.analogy: Like a thin, removable transparent layer placed over a map, instead of redrawing the whole map.
nuance.etymology: Short for Low-Rank Adaptation, the name the Microsoft researchers gave the technique in their 2021 paper.
common_mistakes: Spelling out L-O-R-A instead of saying the word LOR-uh.
Treating LoRA as any kind of adapter; LoRA names one specific low-rank method.

conversation.text: LoRA freezes the original weights and learns a pair of low-rank matrices whose product is added to them.
After training, the LoRA update can be merged into the base weights, so there's no extra inference latency.
What rank did you use for the LoRA adapters? Rank 8 might be too small for this task.

senses.definition: A cradlesong, a soothing song to calm children or lull them to sleep.
senses.example: sing a lullaby

senses.definition: To sing a lullaby to.
senses.example: She would lullaby the baby softly until his eyes finally closed.

core.definition: A soft, soothing song sung to a baby or young child to help them fall asleep.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle syllable to a weak 'uh', so it sounds like 'luh' rather than 'lee'. End with 'bye', rhyming with 'sky'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: It is warm and gentle, suggesting comfort, care and bedtime.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lullaby for a soft song sung to babies, often by a parent at bedtime, and sometimes for any calming tune. Rock-a-bye Baby is a widely known American lullaby. For a rhyme that is spoken rather than sung, say nursery rhyme or bedtime rhyme.

distinctions.note: A nursery rhyme is usually spoken or chanted with a playful rhythm, while a lullaby is sung slowly and softly to make a child sleep.
A cradle song is an older or literary name for a lullaby, rarely used in everyday American speech.

examples.everyday: My mom used to sing me a lullaby every night before I went to bed.
examples.professional: For the baby monitor app, we chose a soft lullaby as the default bedtime sound.
examples.analytical: The lullaby calms a child through its soothing repetition, making the world briefly predictable and safe.

nuance.analogy: Like a slow rocking chair set to music, easing a child gently toward sleep.
nuance.etymology: From lull (to soothe to sleep) and the interjection bye, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in luh-luh-BYE.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'lee' rather than a reduced 'luh'.

senses.definition: Initialism of lookup table.

core.definition: A lookup table: a stored list of precomputed values that a program reads directly instead of computing each result again.

pronunciation.tip: Say each letter by its name, L-U-T, with the primary stress on the last letter, as in 'el yoo TEE'. Don't run the letters together into one word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use LUT mainly in software, graphics, video, and hardware work. With nontechnical people, colleagues usually say 'lookup table' in full. In video and color work, LUT often means a color lookup table used to grade footage.

distinctions.note: LUT is the abbreviation; the full term is used when speaking to nonspecialists or at a document's first mention.
A hash table finds keys by computing a hash, while a LUT is usually a simpler indexed array with direct access.

collocations: store the values in a LUT
apply a LUT to the footage

examples.everyday: My video editor said the color grade is just a LUT, so I can swap it in a second.
examples.professional: We can cut the computation time by storing the values in a LUT at startup.
examples.analytical: Replacing repeated calculations with a LUT trades memory for speed, which matters most when the function is expensive.

nuance.analogy: Like a cheat sheet of answers you memorize before a test: you look them up instead of solving each one again.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of 'lookup table', from look up plus table; the letters are spoken one by one.
common_mistakes: Saying it as the word 'lut' or 'loot'; say the letters L-U-T.
Using LUT for any database; it usually means an indexed array of precomputed results.

senses.definition: To enjoy luxury, to indulge.
senses.example: Luxuriate in the wonderful service of our five-star hotel.

senses.definition: To be luxuriant; to grow exuberantly.
senses.example: Vines luxuriated along the fence after the spring rains, thick and green.

core.definition: To relax and take great pleasure in something comfortable, pleasant or luxurious, such as a warm bath or the sun.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the ZHOOR syllable, and the middle is a reduced 'ur' sound, not 'OO-ur-ate'. End with a clear 'ayt' like 'ate', not 'it'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes pleasure taken in comfort, often with a sense of slow, unhurried enjoyment. The second, rare sense (to grow lushly, as plants do) is seldom used today.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use luxuriate mostly in writing or in a slightly playful spoken way, as in 'I luxuriated in a long bath.' It sounds more elegant than 'enjoy' and is less common than 'relax' in casual talk. It is almost always followed by 'in', so you say 'luxuriate in the sun' rather than 'luxuriate the sun.'

distinctions.note: Bask suggests lying in warmth or approval and is more physical or emotional in tone; luxuriate suggests slow, indulgent enjoyment of comfort in general.
Indulge means to allow yourself something pleasant, often food or a treat; luxuriate focuses on lingering over the pleasure rather than on the act of giving in.

examples.everyday: After the long hike, I luxuriated in a hot shower for almost half an hour.
examples.professional: We closed the quarter early, so I plan to luxuriate in a free afternoon before the next sprint planning.
examples.analytical: Seneca warned that those who luxuriate in comfort gradually lose the strength to endure hardship.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat stretched out in a patch of sunlight, slowly and completely enjoying the warmth.
nuance.etymology: From Latin luxuriare, 'to grow rank or excessively,' from luxuria, 'excess' or 'luxury'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'luxuriate the bath' or 'luxuriate the sun' instead of 'luxuriate in'.
Pronouncing it with a 'k' sound, as in 'LUK-shur-ate'; the 'x' here is /gʒ/.

luxuriate.etymology: Latin *lūxuriātus*, perfect passive participle of *lūxuriō*, see *-ate*.

senses.definition: A clever scheme or artful plot, usually crafted for evil purposes.
The act of machinating or plotting.
senses.example: Her rivals' machinations to oust her from the board were exposed in a leaked email.

senses.definition: 1 2 “machination, n.”, in OED Online ⁠, Oxford: Oxford University Press, launched 2000.

core.definition: A clever, secret scheme or plot, usually designed to harm someone or gain power unfairly.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -nay- and the ending -tion is pronounced 'shun.' Do not reduce the 'a' in -nay- to a schwa; it is a full, long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests cunning, deception, and hidden motives.
nuance.usage_note: Americans typically use machination in newspapers, political writing, historical discussion, or serious debate about intrigue. In everyday speech, they would say 'scheme' or 'plot' instead. The plural machinations is common and often appears in phrases like 'political machinations.'

distinctions.note: Scheme is everyday and can be neutral or positive. Machination is formal and almost always negative.
Plot can refer to a story's structure or to a secret plan. Machination focuses on the cleverness and deviousness of the scheme.

examples.everyday: My uncle was convinced that the whole neighborhood meeting was just a machination to raise property taxes.
examples.professional: We need to look past the machinations in the vendor's proposal, because the cheap price hides hidden fees.
examples.analytical: Milton's account of Satan depicts his machinations as a corruption of reason, aimed at turning human freedom against itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of gears hidden inside a clock, the machination works out of sight, and only its ticking outcome becomes visible.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin machinatio, 'a contriving,' from machinari, 'to contrive,' related to Latin machina, 'machine.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'machine' in pronunciation or meaning; the word is about scheming, not mechanics.
Using the singular where the plural 'machinations' is natural for ongoing schemes.

machination.etymology: From Middle English *machynacion,machynacyon*, from Middle French *machination* and directly Latin *machinatio*, from *māchinor* (“devise, invent”).

senses.definition: Master; sir: a title used in the Middle Ages, given to a person in authority, or to one having a license from a university to teach philosophy and the liberal arts.
The possessor of a master's degree.
senses.example: She earned her magister in theology at the university before starting her doctorate.

senses.definition: The chief male celebrant of an occult ritual.
senses.example: In the novel, the magister led the midnight ritual, chanting in a candlelit cellar.

core.definition: A master or teacher; in the Middle Ages, a title for a person licensed by a university to teach philosophy and the liberal arts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-er' is rhotic and unstressed, so say it as a soft 'ur' with the r clearly sounded.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly pompous. In modern use it sounds scholarly or old-fashioned and can seem showy if used for an ordinary teacher.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'magister' in everyday speech. You will meet it mainly in histories of medieval universities, in discussions of European degrees, and in Latin phrases such as 'magister artium' (Master of Arts). For a normal teacher or boss, say 'teacher' or 'mentor'. In a joking tone, a friend might call a know-it-all 'the magister'.

distinctions.note: 'Master' is the everyday word for a skilled person or a teacher. 'Magister' is a learned, historical academic title.
A magistrate is an official who administers the law, often a judge in a lower court. A magister is a licensed teacher or scholar.

examples.professional: Our German colleague holds a Magister degree, which is roughly equivalent to a master's, so HR accepted it for the position.
examples.analytical: In medieval Paris, a candidate could not teach in the faculty of arts until he had been admitted as a magister by the university.

nuance.analogy: A magister is like a licensed guild master in the medieval world, the person formally certified to pass on a craft.
nuance.etymology: From Latin magister, master or chief, from magis, more.
common_mistakes: Using 'magister' as a casual word for any teacher, which sounds archaic or pretentious in American speech.
Confusing it with 'magistrate', which is a different word with a different meaning.

magister.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *magister* (“a master, chief, head, superior, director, teacher, etc.”), from *magis* (“more or great”) + *-ter*.

senses.definition: A judicial officer with limited authority to administer and enforce the law. A magistrate's court may have jurisdiction in civil or criminal cases, or both.
A comparable official in medieval or modern institutions.
senses.example: Like other civil servants, Ashok Kumar started his career as an Assistant Collector cum Sub-divisional Magistrate.

senses.definition: A master's degree.
senses.example: After three years of study, she finally earned her magistrate in theology.

senses.definition: (historical) A high official of the state or a municipality in ancient Greece or Rome.
senses.example: In ancient Rome, a magistrate could issue edicts and command legions in the field.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A public official with limited judicial power who hears minor criminal and civil cases and can enforce the law locally.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAJ, and make the final syllable rhyme with 'gate', not 'it'. In American speech the 'a' sounds like 'ay' even in an unstressed-looking position, so say 'strayt' clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names an official role, and the word may sound serious when used about someone in trouble with the law.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use magistrate mainly for judges in local or lower courts, such as a small-claims or traffic court. In the US a magistrate judge is usually a federal official who assists district judges, so the title can differ by court. Most people say 'judge' in everyday talk, but 'magistrate' is correct when speaking formally about a lower-level court officer.

distinctions.note: A judge usually has full authority in a court; a magistrate often has narrower powers, such as setting bail or hearing minor cases.
Justice is a judge on a state supreme court or the U.S. Supreme Court; magistrate is a lower-ranking officer.

examples.everyday: I had to go to traffic court, and the magistrate reduced my fine.
examples.professional: The clerk will file the warrant request with the magistrate before the hearing.
examples.analytical: The distinction between a magistrate and a judge reflects a historical split between local discretion and centralized judicial authority.

nuance.analogy: A magistrate is like a first-round referee in a sports league: they make the early calls and can end minor matters, but the final decisions on serious cases go to the head officials.
nuance.etymology: From Latin magistratus, 'office of a magistrate', from magister, 'master'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable as 'it' instead of 'ayt'.
Using magistrate as a general word for any judge in American courts.
Stressing the second syllable, which sounds unnatural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, Greek words for rulers and officials appear in several passages. In Acts 16:20-22, 35-38, the city officials of Philippi, called strategoi, order Paul and Silas beaten and later release them, and the RSV renders these officials as magistrates. Romans 13:3-4 speaks of rulers (Greek archontes) as God's servants who bear the sword against wrongdoing, and Titus 3:1 tells Christians to be subject to rulers and authorities.

magistrate.etymology: From Middle English *magistrat* (“magistrate; magistracy”), borrowed from Latin *magistrātus*.

senses.definition: An instrument made of convex glass, used to magnify.
senses.example: He used a magnifying glass to read the tiny serial number stamped inside the watch case.

core.definition: A handheld lens that makes small print, objects or details look larger so they are easier to see.

pronunciation.tip: In the phrase, the main stress falls on GLASS, but the word magnifying has its own stress on MAG-, so say both stresses clearly. Don't reduce the -ing to 'in' in careful speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical; it can also suggest careful scrutiny.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use magnifying glass in everyday talk for reading fine print or looking at small things like stamps, insects or a splinter. The phrase 'under a magnifying glass' means being examined very closely, often by critics or the media. Someone might say 'Hand me that magnifying glass' or 'Can you use the magnifying glass?' and the natural reply is 'Sure, here you go.'

distinctions.note: Magnifier is a broader and more technical term, while magnifying glass is the common everyday phrase for the handheld lens.
A microscope uses multiple lenses to view very small objects, while a magnifying glass uses a single lens and gives lower magnification.

examples.everyday: I need a magnifying glass to read the directions on this medicine bottle.
examples.professional: Put the sample under the lab's magnifying glass and tell me what you see along the edge.
examples.analytical: Historians often examine one document under a magnifying glass, which reveals fine detail but can distort the larger context.

nuance.analogy: A magnifying glass is a window with a curved bulge that bends light so the same view looks bigger.
nuance.etymology: Magnifying is from magnify, from Latin magnificare, and glass is from Old English glæs.
common_mistakes: Saying 'magnify glass' without the -ing; the correct phrase is magnifying glass.
Using the plural 'magnifying glasses' when you mean a single lens, or using the singular when you mean a pair.

senses.definition: In a syllogism, the term that is the predicate of the conclusion.

core.definition: In a syllogism, the term that functions as the predicate of the conclusion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TERM, the second word, with a strong, rhotic 'er' vowel as in 'turn.' The first word 'major' is weaker, so say 'may-jer TURM.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term almost exclusively in logic, philosophy, and rhetoric courses, where it names one part of a categorical syllogism. Outside those settings, most people would not recognize it. Students should be ready to identify the major term, minor term, and middle term when analyzing an argument.

distinctions.note: The major premise is a whole proposition that contains the major term, while the major term is only one of the three terms.
The minor term is the subject of the conclusion, while the major term is the predicate of the conclusion.

collocations: the major term of a syllogism

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor kept asking us to name the major term, and I still couldn't keep the three terms straight.
examples.professional: In our logic training module, we check each syllogism by first mapping the major term to the predicate of the conclusion.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's classification of syllogisms depends on the position of the major term, which determines whether the argument is valid under a given figure.

nuance.analogy: In a syllogism the major term is like the destination of a road trip: it is where the conclusion finally arrives.
nuance.etymology: 'Major' from Latin maior, 'greater'; 'term' from Latin terminus, 'end' or 'boundary.'
common_mistakes: Confusing the major term with the major premise, which is a whole proposition containing the term.
Mixing up the major term with the minor term, which is the subject of the conclusion.
Mispronouncing 'term' with a short 'e' vowel instead of the rhotic 'er' sound.

senses.definition: A person who applies makeup and prosthetics for theatrical, television, film, fashion, magazines and similar productions.

core.definition: A person who applies makeup and prosthetics for films, television, theater, fashion shoots, and similar productions.

pronunciation.tip: In the noun, the stress falls on MAKE, the first word, and the compound is said as 'MAYK-up,' not 'make UP,' which is the verb. ARTIST has a lighter secondary stress and a reduced final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive to neutral. It describes a creative, skilled profession, and people usually respond with interest.
nuance.usage_note: Americans write 'makeup' as one word for the noun and use 'make up' as two words for the verb. In the film and television industry, a 'key makeup artist' leads the department, and 'MUA' is a common abbreviation. A natural reply is 'That sounds like a fun job.'

distinctions.note: A cosmetologist is a licensed beauty professional with broader training, while a makeup artist focuses on applying makeup, often for performance or photography.
A hair stylist works on hair, while a makeup artist works on the face and skin, often with a team on a set.

collocations: makeup artist for a music video

examples.everyday: My cousin is a makeup artist, so she did my makeup for the wedding and it looked amazing.
examples.professional: The production hired a makeup artist to age the actors for the flashback scenes.
examples.analytical: The makeup artist's craft shapes the audience's sense of character, turning the body into a canvas for narrative meaning.

nuance.analogy: Like a set designer for the face: the artist builds the look that the camera will see, just as a set designer builds the scene.
nuance.etymology: 'Make up' from Old English macian and up; 'artist' from Italian artista.
common_mistakes: Writing 'make up artist' as two words in the noun form, when 'makeup artist' is standard.
Stressing UP in the noun, as in 'make UP artist,' instead of 'MAKE-up artist.'

core.definition: Wealth or material possessions, especially when pursued as a selfish goal or treated as a rival to God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MAM. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'un', not 'ohn'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in religious and moral contexts. It suggests greed and the worship of money.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mammon mostly in sermons, religious writing, and literary discussions of greed. In everyday speech they would say 'money', 'wealth', or 'materialism'. Using it casually may sound preachy or old-fashioned, though it can be a witty way to mock greed.

distinctions.note: Wealth is a neutral term for riches, while mammon carries a moral judgment against valuing money above God or others.
Materialism is a philosophical or social term for valuing possessions, while mammon is a more vivid, religious word for greed.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the company only cares about profit, that it is just serving mammon.
examples.professional: The leadership retreat asked us to reflect on whether our bonus targets encourage mammon over service to customers.
examples.analytical: Christian ethicists have long used mammon as a symbol of the rival loyalty that competes with devotion to God.

nuance.analogy: Mammon is like a jealous master: once you serve money, it demands all your attention and loyalty.
nuance.etymology: From Aramaic mamona and Greek mammonas, meaning 'wealth, riches'.
common_mistakes: Treating mammon as a neutral synonym for money, when it has a strong moral sense.
Pronouncing it as 'MAY-mon' with a long a.
nuance.biblical_note: Mammon comes from Aramaic mamona and Greek mammonas, meaning wealth or riches. In the New Testament Jesus uses it to describe material possessions as a rival to God. In Matthew 6:24 he says that no one can serve two masters, and that you cannot serve God and mammon. Luke 16:13 repeats this teaching, and Luke 16:9-11 speaks of the unrighteous mammon, urging people to use wealth wisely.

senses.definition: Evident to the senses, especially to the sight; apparent; distinctly perceived.
senses.example: Her disappointment was manifest in her silence and her folded arms.

senses.definition: Obvious to the understanding; apparent to the mind; easily apprehensible; plain; not obscure or hidden.
senses.example: Her error was manifest to anyone who checked the arithmetic.

senses.definition: (rare) Detected; convicted.
senses.example: The fraud was manifest once the auditors traced every forged signature.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A list or invoice of the passengers or goods being carried by a commercial vehicle or ship.
senses.example: ship's manifest

senses.definition: A file containing metadata describing other files.
senses.example: The package includes a manifest listing every file and its checksum.

senses.definition: To show plainly; to make to appear distinctly, usually to the mind; to put beyond question or doubt; to display; to exhibit.
senses.example: His courage manifested itself through the look on his face.

senses.definition: To become manifest; to be revealed.
senses.example: His osteoporosis first manifested as pain in his hips.

senses.definition: To will something to exist.
senses.example: Through prayer, she believed she could manifest a new job within a month.

senses.definition: To exhibit the manifests or prepared invoices of; to declare at the customhouse.
senses.example: The captain must manifest the cargo at customs before the ship docks.

core.definition: Clear and easy to see or understand; obvious to anyone who looks or thinks about it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAN. The middle syllable is a reduced vowel, so say 'ih' quickly, and the final 'est' is unstressed and short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds formal and emphasizes that something is clearly visible or evident.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'manifest' mostly in writing, speeches, and formal discussion. In casual talk, people say 'obvious', 'clear', or 'plain to see'. The phrase 'manifest destiny' is a historical American term about westward expansion in the 1800s.

distinctions.note: Obvious is common everyday English, while manifest is formal and often suggests something made visible or demonstrated.
Apparent often means seemingly true but possibly not, while manifest means clearly and undeniably evident.

examples.everyday: It was manifest from the look on his face that he was not happy with the result.
examples.professional: The manifest error in the report was caught before it went to the client.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the moral consequences of the policy are manifest in its failure to protect the most vulnerable.

nuance.analogy: A manifest truth is like a sign written in large letters on a highway: anyone passing by can read it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'manifestus', meaning caught in the act, plain, or palpable.
common_mistakes: Using 'manifest' as a simple synonym for 'manifested' or 'show', as in 'He manifest his anger' (correct as a verb but often replaced by 'showed').
Confusing it with 'manifesto', a public statement of principles.

manifest.etymology: From Middle English *manifest*, *manifeste*, from Latin *manifestus*, *manufestus* (“palpable, manifest”), from Latin *manus* (“hand”) + an uncertain second element.

senses.definition: In a martial manner.

core.definition: In a way that suggests soldiers, war, or military discipline; in a military or warlike manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MAR. The 'tial' is pronounced 'shul', as in 'partial', not 'tee-ul'. The final syllable is a light 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral or negative. It describes a bearing or manner that is stern, forceful, or aggressive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'martially' in everyday speech. You will mostly see it in literary writing, music descriptions such as 'martial music', or formal description of posture or manner. For military action, Americans say 'militarily', not 'martially'.

distinctions.note: Militarily concerns military action, forces, or strategy. Martially describes a manner or style that suggests soldiers or military discipline.
Warlike is a plainer adjective describing a tendency toward war. Martially is an adverb describing how someone acts or moves.

examples.everyday: The drum corps marched martially down Main Street on the Fourth of July, and everyone cheered.
examples.professional: The new guard's posture was too martially rigid for a role that depends on warm customer relationships.
examples.analytical: The poem's refrain beats martially, turning private grief into a public call to arms.

nuance.analogy: Acting martially is like standing at attention, with every movement sharp and deliberate.
nuance.etymology: From martial, from Latin martialis, 'of Mars, god of war', plus the suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'tee' instead of 'shul'.
Using 'martially' to mean militarily, as in 'martially defeated the enemy'.

senses.definition: The killing of a large number of people over a short period of time.

core.definition: The deliberate killing of a large number of people within a short period, often in one attack or event.

pronunciation.tip: The first word carries the main stress, and the second word is weakly stressed. The ur in murder is a strong r-colored vowel, so say it as a clear er sound.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes one of the most serious crimes, used with shock and grief.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mass murder in news, legal, political and everyday talk about violent attacks on many people. Mass shooting is more common for gun attacks, and genocide is used when a group is targeted for destruction. Mass murder is a serious term, so do not use it casually about small incidents.

distinctions.note: Genocide means killing people because they belong to a national, ethnic or religious group with the intent to destroy that group; mass murder does not require that motive.
Serial murder involves separate killings over time, usually by one person, while mass murder involves many killed in a short period.

collocations: a mass murder in a school

examples.everyday: I can't believe the news about that mass murder downtown, and I keep thinking about the families.
examples.professional: Our crisis plan covers how to respond to a mass murder or active shooter incident on campus.
examples.analytical: Philosophers debate whether mass murder is morally distinct from genocide or merely a larger number of individual wrongs.

nuance.etymology: Combines mass, from Latin massa meaning lump, and murder, from Old English morthor.
common_mistakes: Stressing both words equally, which makes the phrase sound flat.
Using mass murder for an ordinary killing with one victim.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a membrane.

core.definition: Of or relating to a membrane, which is a thin layer of tissue or material that covers, lines, or separates parts of the body or a cell.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MEM. The an in membranal is reduced to uh, unlike the long ay sound in the noun membrane (MEM-brayn).

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Biologists and medical writers use this word occasionally, but Americans more often write 'membrane' as a noun modifier, as in 'membrane protein', or use 'membranous'. In everyday English you are unlikely to hear this word, so save it for technical reading or precise academic writing.

distinctions.note: Membranous is far more common and can describe texture, as in thin and pliable, while membranal simply means relating to a membrane.
Membrane is the noun for the thin layer itself, while membranal is the adjective describing its relation to that layer.

examples.everyday: When you peel a hard-boiled egg, that thin inner skin is what a biologist would call membranal tissue.
examples.professional: The sample showed a membranal layer that stained differently from the surrounding cytoplasm, so we flagged it for review.
examples.analytical: Calling the boundary membranal stresses its relation to the membrane itself, rather than its thin, pliable texture.

nuance.analogy: A membranal layer is like the skin of a balloon: it separates one space from another while letting some things pass through.
nuance.etymology: From membrane, from Latin membrana, 'skin or covering', plus the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using membranal to mean thin and transparent; that quality is better described by membranous.
Stressing the second syllable, as in mem-BRAN-al, when the stress belongs on the first syllable.

senses.definition: A ship that is principally or (usually) entirely civilian, engaged in trade, which carries cargo, passengers, or both.

core.definition: A privately owned, civilian ship that carries cargo or passengers for trade rather than a military ship.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SHIP, with secondary stress on the first syllable of merchant. The middle syllable reduces to a short 'chunt', and the words link smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a maritime term, and in ordinary talk people often say cargo ship instead.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use merchant ship mostly in naval history, shipping news and discussions of the U.S. Merchant Marine. In everyday talk, a cargo ship or container ship is more common. In news coverage, 'civilian vessel' is also used.

distinctions.note: A cargo ship is designed to carry freight, while merchant ship is broader and includes passenger ships, meaning any civilian ship engaged in trade.
A warship is armed and part of a navy, while a merchant ship is civilian even if it is used in wartime and may be attacked.

examples.everyday: My grandfather spent years on a merchant ship, so he always talked about the ports he visited.
examples.professional: The insurer needs the merchant ship's cargo manifest before it can process the claim.
examples.analytical: The merchant ship, unlike the warship, depends on commercial law and neutrality to move its goods across contested waters.

nuance.analogy: A merchant ship is a delivery truck on the water: it carries other people's goods for a fee, not weapons.
nuance.etymology: From merchant (from Old French marchant, trader) plus ship (from Old English scip).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable of merchant; say MUR-chunt.
Confusing merchant ship with merchant marine: the marine is the whole civilian fleet and its sailors, while a merchant ship is one vessel.

core.definition: A common Hebrew personal name in the Bible, borne by several men, including leaders of the returned exiles and workers on Jerusalem's walls.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SHOO. Keep the final syllable light, with a reduced vowel, rather than saying it as LAM.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this name outside of Bible reading, genealogy or scholarship. When the name appears in a list, readers often need the father's name to tell the men apart. Most people simply say it as the name of a biblical figure.

examples.everyday: My study Bible lists three different men named Meshullam, so I had to check which one is meant.
examples.professional: The archive lists several Meshullams, so we must check each one's father's name before identifying him.
examples.analytical: Because Meshullam recurs across Ezra, Nehemiah and Kings, the genealogies show how shared names were distinguished by family lineage.

nuance.etymology: Hebrew personal name, traditionally linked to a root meaning to repay or make whole; the exact sense is debated.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable
Assuming all men named Meshullam are the same person
nuance.biblical_note: Meshullam is a Hebrew personal name borne by several men in the Old Testament. One Meshullam, son of Berechiah, helped repair the wall of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:4). Another is among the leaders sent to gather Levites for the return from exile (Ezra 8:16). The name also appears in the line of Shaphan, the royal secretary (2 Kings 22:3), so readers must check the family line to identify each man.

senses.definition: In a metonymic fashion; using metonymy.
senses.example: The headline referred metonymically to the crown when it meant the whole royal government.

core.definition: In a way that uses metonymy, naming something by a word for a closely related thing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NIM, as in the adjective. The -ically ending reduces to 'ik-lee', with the -ly as a clear 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise analytical term.
nuance.usage_note: This adverb appears almost only in literary criticism, linguistics and rhetoric writing, as in 'the phrase is used metonymically.' Americans rarely use it in conversation. In speech, a simpler phrase such as 'they are using it as a stand-in' works better.

distinctions.note: Figuratively is the general term for any non-literal language; metonymically names one specific device.
Metaphorically means comparing by resemblance; metonymically means substituting by association or closeness.

examples.everyday: When people say 'the Hill' in Washington, they are talking metonymically about Congress.
examples.professional: In the memo, 'engineering' is used metonymically for the team leads, so we should clarify exactly who is meant.
examples.analytical: The poet refers metonymically to the throne, meaning the monarch's authority rather than the chair itself.

nuance.analogy: Using a word metonymically is like pointing to a neighbor's car to mean the neighbor: the object stands in for the person.
nuance.etymology: From metonymy, from Greek metōnymia, 'change of name', with the adverb suffix -ically.
common_mistakes: Confusing metonymically with metaphorically, which is about comparison rather than association
Putting the stress on the wrong syllable; it is met-uh-NIM-ik-lee
Using the word in casual conversation where a simpler phrase sounds more natural

senses.definition: To manage, direct, or control a person, group, or system to an unnecessary level of detail or precision.
senses.example: The employees complained that their boss was micromanaging when she insisted that they account for their time in fifteen-minute intervals.

core.definition: To control every detail of someone's work, rather than giving them room to decide how to do it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on "MAN" in the middle, not on "MY." The last syllable is "-ij," the same sound as in "manage," so don't say a long "-aj" ending.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a boss or manager who is too controlling and does not trust others to do their job.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word a lot in workplace conversation, often when complaining about a boss or describing a management problem. It is common in both written and spoken English, from emails to coffee-break talk. To describe a helpful, hands-off style, people often say the manager "gives people room" or "trusts the team."

distinctions.note: Supervising means overseeing work in a normal way, while micromanaging means controlling every small detail, which is usually seen as excessive.
Delegating means handing over a task and trusting someone to complete it, which is the opposite of micromanaging.

examples.everyday: My brother quit his job because his boss kept micromanaging every little thing he did at home.
examples.professional: I try not to micromanage my team, so I set clear goals and let them decide how to reach them.
examples.analytical: Micromanaging often reflects a failure of trust, because the manager substitutes control over process for confidence in outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Micromanaging is like a driving instructor who grabs the steering wheel every time you turn, so you never learn to drive yourself.
nuance.etymology: From "micro-" (small, from Greek mikros) plus "manage," meaning to control or direct.
common_mistakes: Using "micromanage" as a neutral word for good supervision. It almost always criticizes too much control.
Saying "micromanage about" or "micromanage on" instead of using the object directly, as in "micromanage the project."

senses.definition: An intermediary, agent between two (or more) parties.
senses.example: act as a middleman

senses.definition: An intermediate dealer between the manufacturer and the retailer or customer.
senses.example: The farmer sold his produce directly to stores without a middleman.

senses.definition: To act as a middleman or intermediary.
senses.example: Rather than negotiating directly, the broker agreed to middleman the sale between the two families.

core.definition: A person or company that buys goods from producers and sells them on to retailers or customers, or that links two parties.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MID. The middle syllable is a syllabic l, so do not add an extra 'e' vowel like 'mid-del-man'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. Consumers often see middlemen as adding cost, though in business they can provide real value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'cut out the middleman' to mean buying directly from the source to save money. The word is used in business, economics and everyday shopping talk. The plural is middlemen, and the verb form is less common.

distinctions.note: A broker arranges deals for a commission, as in stock broker or insurance broker, while middleman is a broader term often used for goods.
Go-between is informal and often refers to someone who carries messages between people, while middleman is more commonly used in business.

examples.everyday: We bought the eggs straight from the farm so there's no middleman taking a cut.
examples.professional: Our platform removes the middleman between freelance designers and small businesses, so the fees go to the creators.
examples.analytical: Economists have long argued that a middleman creates real value by reducing search costs, though critics see only an added markup.

nuance.analogy: A middleman is like a waiter between you and the kitchen: he carries the order, takes a share, and sometimes adds his own price.
nuance.etymology: Middle comes from Old English middel, and man comes from Old English man, a person.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, 'middle man', in a noun sense; the standard American form is one word.
Using the plural 'middleman' instead of 'middlemen'.

middleman.etymology: From Middle English *myddil man*, equivalent to *middle* + *man*.

senses.definition: A point equidistant between two extremes.
A point which divides a line segment into two lines of equal length.
senses.example: Draw a line from the corner to the midpoint of the opposite side.

senses.definition: Synonym of middle dot.

core.definition: A point exactly halfway between two ends, or the middle point of a line segment or a process.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MID, and keep the 'oy' in 'point' as a clear diphthong like the vowel in 'coin'. Do not say it like 'mid-pint', which rhymes with 'pint'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise; sometimes used figuratively for the turning point of a process.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use midpoint in everyday talk for the halfway mark of a trip, project or game, and in math for the center of a line segment. In casual speech people often say halfway or the middle, but midpoint sounds more deliberate and fits meetings and reports well. It is a neutral word suitable for business writing and classroom explanations.

distinctions.note: Center is the middle of a region or object; midpoint is the point halfway along a line or sequence.
Halfway is an everyday adverb or adjective, as in halfway there; midpoint is the noun for the exact point.
Midway usually works as an adverb or adjective for the middle of a distance; midpoint is the more precise noun.

examples.everyday: We're at the midpoint of the hike, so let's stop for some water.
examples.professional: We hit the midpoint of the migration, so the next status update should cover the rollback plan.
examples.analytical: The midpoint of the argument is the claim that moral value cannot be reduced to utility, and the rest of the essay defends it.

nuance.analogy: A midpoint is like the fulcrum of a seesaw: equal distance on each side.
nuance.etymology: From mid (middle) and point.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'mid-pint', as if it rhymes with 'pint'.
Using midpoint for any middle; it refers to a precise point along a line or sequence.

senses.definition: In a mischievous manner.

core.definition: In a playful way that is meant to tease or cause small, harmless trouble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'MIS', not on the 'chie' part. The word has three syllables in American speech, with the middle 'ous' becoming a quick 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Positive to neutral; it suggests playful teasing rather than real harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use this adverb after verbs of looking or smiling, such as 'grinned mischievously' or 'winked mischievously'. It sounds natural in storytelling, friendly conversation and writing. It describes playful intent, so it is a poor choice for describing serious wrongdoing, where 'maliciously' is the better word.

distinctions.note: Playfully is broader and can mean simply in a lighthearted way, while mischievously adds the idea of teasing or causing small trouble.
Maliciously means with intent to harm, which is much more negative than mischievously.

examples.everyday: She grinned mischievously and reached for the last slice of pie before anyone else noticed.
examples.professional: The presenter winked mischievously and said the budget had a surprise in store for the team.
examples.analytical: The narrator addresses the reader mischievously, undermining the very authority he claims to possess.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat sitting near a bowl of milk: it looks innocent, but you know it is planning something small.
nuance.etymology: From 'mischievous', from Anglo-French 'meschevous', from 'mischief', plus the adverbial '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the 'chie' syllable, as in 'mis-CHEE-vus-ly'; the stress belongs on 'MIS'.
Misspelling it as 'mischeviously'; the 'ie' appears again before the 'ous' ending.

senses.definition: A collection containing a variety of miscellaneous things.
senses.example: His garage was a mishmash of old bicycles, paint cans, and mismatched lamps nobody had touched in years.

senses.definition: To mix together, especially in a confused way.
senses.example: Try not to mishmash the research notes with the budget spreadsheets, or nobody will find anything.

senses.definition: To become mixed together.
senses.example: After the two bands shared a stage all summer, their sounds began to mishmash into something new.

core.definition: A confused or messy mixture of many different things, often with no clear order or pattern.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable has the short a of 'cat,' so it rhymes with 'clash' rather than 'mosh.' Keep the 'sh' sound clear and do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it suggests a jumble that lacks order, though it can be affectionate for a cheerful mix of things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mishmash in casual speech and writing to describe a jumble of ideas, styles, foods or objects, such as 'a mishmash of genres' or 'a mishmash of leftovers.' It is informal and playful, so avoid it in formal reports where 'mixture' or 'hodgepodge' fits better. The verb form is less common in everyday American speech than the noun.

distinctions.note: Hodgepodge is nearly identical in meaning and slightly more common in American writing, but mishmash has a more playful, reduplicated sound.
Mixture is neutral and can describe a deliberate blend, while mishmash implies something confused and unplanned.
A medley is a pleasant combination, often of songs or pieces, while a mishmash suggests disorder.

examples.everyday: Our hotel room was a mishmash of old couches and mismatched lamps, but it was charming.
examples.professional: The slide deck is a mishmash of charts from three different projects, so let's rebuild it before Friday.
examples.analytical: The essay reads as a mishmash of incompatible philosophies rather than a single coherent argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a junk drawer where batteries, string, receipts and old keys all live together with no system.
nuance.etymology: Reduplicated echo formation based on the English word mash, first recorded in the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, which makes it sound like 'mish-MASH.'
Using mishmash for a deliberate, well-organized combination; it implies confusion.

mishmash.etymology: Attested since the late 15th century, Middle English *mysse masche*, probably a reduplication of *mash*, although a Yiddish origin or influence has also been suggested.

senses.definition: In AI: A type of data a model handles, such as text, images, audio or video.
A particular way in which the information is to be encoded for presentation to humans, i.e. to the type of sign and to the status of reality ascribed to or claimed by a sign, text or genre.
senses.example: The team tested whether modality affected how well users remembered the alerts they saw.

senses.definition: The inflection of a verb that shows how its action is conceived by the speaker.
senses.example: The verb's modality in the sentence shows that the speaker considers the action possible, not certain.

senses.definition: The way in which infrastructure and knowledge of how to use it give rise to a meaningful pattern of interaction (a concept in Anthony Giddens's structuration theory).
senses.example: In structuration theory, modality describes how rules and resources shape everyday social interaction.

senses.definition: The subject concerning certain diatonic scales known as musical modes.
senses.example: The composer built the piece on the Dorian modality, giving it a melancholy, folk-like sound.

senses.definition: Any of the senses (such as sight or taste)
senses.example: Each sensory modality, such as sight or taste, sends signals to a distinct region of the brain.

senses.definition: The classification of propositions on the basis on whether they claim possibility, impossibility, contingency or necessity; mode.
senses.example: In philosophy class, we classified each claim by its modality: possible, impossible, contingent, or necessary.

senses.definition: The fact of being modal.
senses.example: In the seminar, we debated whether the modality of a statement can be separated from its content.

senses.definition: The organization and structure of the church, as distinct from sodality or parachurch organizations.
senses.example: The bishop explained the modality of the church, distinguishing parish structure from parachurch ministries.

senses.definition: The quality of being limited by a condition.
That whether a zodiac sign is cardinal, fixed or mutable.
senses.example: The astrologer noted that her Scorpio sun sign has a fixed modality, unlike the cardinal Aries.

senses.definition: A method of diagnosis or therapy.
senses.example: The clinic offered several therapy modalities, including physical therapy, acupuncture, and ultrasound treatment.

core.definition: In AI, a type of data that a model processes, such as text, images, audio or video.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'DA'. The middle 'a' is a weak vowel, and the final '-ty' is a flapped 't' that sounds like 'dee' in fast American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in AI and a philosophical term in semiotics.
nuance.usage_note: In AI, Americans use 'modality' for the type of input or output, as in 'a text-only model' or 'a multimodal model'. In philosophy and linguistics, the word can mean how a sign claims reality or how a speaker expresses possibility. In everyday speech, Americans say 'mode' or 'type' instead, and in grammar they say 'mood'.

distinctions.note: A 'mode' is a general way of operating; 'modality' in AI refers specifically to the kind of data being processed.
'Multimodal' describes a system that handles more than one modality, such as text plus images.

examples.everyday: My phone's assistant handles voice, but the new one also works with images, so it covers more modalities.
examples.professional: Our model handles text and images in one pipeline, so we need to test robustness across both modalities.
examples.analytical: Each genre carries its own modality, the degree to which a text claims to represent reality, and this claim shapes how readers interpret it.

nuance.analogy: A modality is like a language a model speaks: text, images or sound each need their own vocabulary.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'modalitas', from 'modus', meaning manner or measure, via medieval Latin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word with a stress on the first syllable, as in 'MOD-al-ity'.
Using 'modality' to mean a single 'mode' of communication; in AI it refers to a category of data.

conversation.text: Each modality, whether text, image, or audio, typically gets its own encoder before the representations are fused.
The model should still work when one modality is missing, like a video without sound.
In medicine, modality can refer to a type of imaging, such as MRI or ultrasound.

senses.definition: The property of being modular.

core.definition: The quality or degree to which a system is made of separate, interchangeable modules that work together through defined interfaces.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on LER, the third syllable, with a secondary stress on the first syllable. The rhotic r is clear, and the final -ity is a reduced ih-tee, not ee-tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; positive when used to praise flexibility, maintainability or reuse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use modularity mainly in software, engineering and systems design, often in meetings or design reviews. It is rarely used in casual conversation.
